extracted.intended_audience: patent policy scholars, USPTO stakeholders, patent attorneys, and academics interested in patent-office empirical research
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the case for changing how much time USPTO patent examiners spend per application, weighing costs, empirical evidence on error rates, and design of reforms or pilots. Focuses on whether increased examiner time (e.g., doubling) is cost-justified and how to implement/evaluate such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination time per application
rubrics_metrics.description: How many hours the USPTO examiner spends evaluating an application (noting the current average of only 19 total hours per application across prosecution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes time for reading submitted materials, searching prior art, writing rejections, and responding to multiple rounds of arguments. The article focuses on the effect of increasing (doubling) that time and the resulting changes in allowances, office actions, and downstream costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit justification for increasing examination effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether spending more examiner time is cost-justified when comparing the additional budgetary cost (e.g., estimated $660 million/year to double time) against savings from reduced litigation and prosecution and broader social benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frakes & Wasserman estimate >$900M in savings from reduced prosecution/litigation; decision should account for both direct budget impacts and broader social costs of erroneous patents. Consider sources of funding (user fees) and how costs compare to the USPTO budget (~$3 billion for patent programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric error risk under time pressure (erroneous allowances vs erroneous rejections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding that time-crunched examiners are more likely to erroneously allow invalid patents than to reject valid ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence comes from changes in examiner behavior after promotion (less time per application), leading to less searching and more allowances; rejections by time-crunched examiners are not more likely to be appealed. This asymmetry is central to claims about litigation savings from more time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art search thoroughness
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality and extent of prior art searching performed by examiners, which depends on available time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promoted examiners who receive less time reportedly spend less time searching prior art and grant more patents. Improving search quality is a direct mechanism by which additional time could reduce erroneous allowances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction in downstream disputes as an outcome metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected decrease in patent grants, patent/lawsuit pairs, and instituted PTAB challenges as measures of the benefit from increased examination time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frakes & Wasserman estimate roughly 80,000 fewer patents granted, 2,400 fewer patent/lawsuit pairs (~$490M savings), and ~270 fewer instituted PTAB challenges (~$110M savings) per year from doubling examiner time. These are illustrative outcome metrics but are based on empirical estimates with assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on prosecution costs and number of office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect of increased examiner time on applicant-side prosecution burden, measured by changes in office actions per application and related costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors predict doubling time would be associated with 0.56 fewer office actions per application, translating to about $300M/year in savings for applicants. Raises the question whether applicants could pay for more thorough initial examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding mechanism and budgetary feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: How additional examination time would be financed (e.g., user fees) and whether the estimate of required funds is plausible relative to USPTO budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doubling time estimated at $660M/year, paid by user fees; consider whether greater efficiency could be achieved without raising fees, and whether the $660M estimate understates total program costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability of empirical estimates and underlying assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the empirical effects observed (for example, around examiner promotions) generalize to broader implementation (hiring more examiners, changing workloads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions include: Can the agency hire additional examiners of similar quality? Are the promotion-based effects representative of marginal changes? How will contemporaneous changes in law and litigation practice alter expected benefits?

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting of additional examination time (which examiners/cases should get more time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding whether extra time should be given universally or targeted to particular examiners, technologies, or cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations include which examiners should get more time, whether focusing on 'compact prosecution' up front helps, and whether marginal dollars are best spent uniformly or targeted to difficult/important cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative or complementary interventions to improve examination quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Other methods besides simply increasing hours that could reduce errors or improve outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options discussed include internal peer review, peer review from outside experts, and providing technical experts within the agency for difficult cases. Evaluate whether these alternatives reduce errors more cost-effectively than additional hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and empirical evaluation of pilot programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing reforms in ways that enable robust empirical evaluation (e.g., randomized pilots) to measure effectiveness before full rollout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO has piloted programs but often not in ways that make rigorous evaluation easy; recommended practices include randomization (including over applicants who opt in) and collaboration with academics to design and evaluate interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to changes in patent law and litigation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: How contemporaneous or future changes in statutory law, case law, or litigation practice affect the expected benefits of increased examination time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should account for legal and procedural context changes that might increase or decrease the value of more thorough examination (e.g., changes in standards for validity challenges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological robustness and uncertainty in empirical estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness that empirical estimates (e.g., savings, reductions in lawsuits) rely on modeling choices and have uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empiricists may quibble with details of methodological choices; sensitivity analyses and transparency about assumptions are necessary when using point estimates (such as the $660M cost or counts of reduced suits) for policy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader social welfare impacts (effects on end users and follow-on innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the social costs imposed by erroneously issued patents via supracompetitive pricing and reduced follow-on innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These broader costs are difficult to quantify but should be included in cost–benefit calculations because invalid patents can impose harms on consumers and subsequent innovators that exceed direct litigation/prosecution savings.
